title: Test the coin
hookLine: test each impression the way a money-changer tests coins (Discourses 1.20)
carry: an impression is a coin someone has passed you

lines: HOW MANY THOUGHTS DID YOU CHECK?
cards: Hand a cashier a hundred-dollar bill and watch. They hold it up to the light, run a pen across it, feel the paper between finger and thumb. Nobody's offended; it's just what you do with money, because fakes exist.
Now think how many thoughts you accepted today without holding a single one up to the light. Epictetus noticed the same mismatch in the markets of his own time.

teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter twenty, on reason examining itself. Every skill, Epictetus says, looks at something outside itself: the cobbler at leather, the musician at sound.
Reason is the one faculty that can look at itself, and at the impressions that come to it.
Then he goes to the market, to the money-changer, whose job is to test coins. For coins, he says, we've invented a whole craft.
The tester uses sight, touch, even smell, and last of all hearing: he drops the coin on the counter and listens to it ring. Not once. Again and again, until his ear is as trained as a musician's.
Where people think a mistake would cost them, they bring every sense to bear.
But the impressions that come to the mind, the passing thought that someone is insulting you, that you're a failure, that you need this thing right now, we accept with a yawn.
Epictetus calls this the philosopher's first and greatest work: to test impressions, and let none in untested.
An impression is a coin someone has passed you. It might be real. It might be lead painted gold.
Before you act on it, say it, or let it set your mood, you can turn it over, hold it to the light, and hear how it rings.

how: Some Stoic practitioners pause on a strong first impression, asking whether it's a fact or an interpretation, before acting on it, a habit some trace to this chapter.

o: a coin-tester: Epictetus' picture for testing thoughts
a banker who lends at interest to people in need
a thief who shaves silver off the edges of coins

games.q: test the coin: tap the pairs.
p: the faculty that looks at itself

s: Epictetus says the money-changer uses only his eyes
sight, touch, smell, and finally hearing the coin ring.
he says we take more care with coins than with our thoughts
with impressions we yawn and accept whatever comes.
for Epictetus, reason is the one faculty that examines itself
other skills look at leather or sound; reason looks at reason.

games.q: you're a money-changer in a Roman market, and someone hands you a coin. what does Epictetus say you do last?
o: drop it and listen to it ring, again and again.
games.why: after sight, touch and smell, the tester listens to the coin ring, until his ear is as trained as a musician's.

practice: Let the next thought that shows up be the coin on the counter: a worry, a judgment about someone, a plan. Is it a fact, or a story about a fact? Is it heavier than it needs to be, and does it ring true or a little hollow?
Then set it down, and wait for the next one.

wordCard.voice: Money-changer. Epictetus' image for testing the mind: the market worker who checks a coin by sight, touch, smell and the ring of its drop, before letting it pass.

orig.note: Greek dokimazō: to test, to assay, the word used for testing metal and coins.

carryVoice: Your line: an impression is a coin someone has passed you. Not every coin is gold. Day four hundred four, done.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.20 (about reason, how it contemplates itself; the money-changer)
